newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: FOCUS-Investor revolt threatens QNI merger.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Investor revolt threatens QNI merger.

text.p: Australian investors angry at what they see as an unfair plan to merge nickel producer QNI Ltd with Gencor Ltd's nickel division could scuttle the A$2.3 billion deal at a shareholders meeting, analysts and brokers said on Friday.

"We came back from their presentation here in Brisbane thinking this is a fantastic deal for Gencor and not good for QNI," said Nick Atkinson, an institutional dealer at Brisbane brokerage Wilson HTM.
"I don't think it will be passed by the shareholders," Atkinson said, adding that QNI may have paid up to three times too much for Gencor's Cerro Matoso nickel mine in Columbia.
"QNI are giving up control of the company for what could be considered at best fair value and they're getting no premium for control," one analyst said.
"I don't think it's going to get through the shareholder meeting," he added.

QNI and the South African-based mining group announced on Wednesday a proposal to merge their nickel operations, with Gencor eventually taking a 56 percent controlling interest in a newly enlarged QNI they said would be worth A$2.3 billion.
The initial reaction was positive as shareholders considered the prospect of their company becoming the world's fourth largest nickel producer.
But analysts views darkened as they assessed the value of Gencor's major nickel asset, the Cerro Matoso mine.

Gencor bought the 46.58 percent of the mine it did not already own from the Columbian government for US$165.8 million in February this year, valuing the complete mine at US$355.95 million or A$475 million.
Gencor's other nickel assets are generally valued by analysts at around A$100 million, putting Gencor's contribution to the joint venture at around $575 million.
Analysts have compared this A$575 million valuation with QNI's A$1.1 billion market capitalisation and wondered why QNI shareholders were getting only 44 percent of the enlarged group.
"It seems that people think QNI paid a hell of a lot of money for the Gencor assets," said BNP Equities head of equities John Bowie Wilson.

This increasing investor anger culminated in a clearly hostile response from analysts and investors at a briefing in Sydney, where QNI was forced to defend the deal and urge them not to reject the merger plan.
"I think it would be a tragedy if we didn't grab this opportunity. Shareholders would be making one hell of a big mistake," QNI managing director Wyn Davies told the briefing.

Davies rejected the valuation of Cerro Matoso mine using the sale of the Columbian government stake in February, saying the mine's planned expansion and low cost profile made such valuations redundant.

He said he could not divulge the valuation QNI used in its negotiations with Gencor, except to say Gencor had valued the mine at A$1.3 billion to A$1.8 billion when it recently considered whether it would sell the mine seperately.
Davies also warned that Gencor was not bluffing and would not come back with a cash takeover bid at a higher price if the merger was rejected.
"They've (Gencor) indicated they are not interested in bidding for the company (if the merger is rejected)," he said.
Analysts were also disappointed the merger would initially dilute earnings per share (EPS) because of high depreciation and amortisation costs.
A QNI official confirmed the expected dilution at the briefing, but said the merger would produce strong EPS growth in the third and fourth years of the new enlarged company.
"It would be about 20 percent in the first year," the official told the briefing.
QNI's shares ended nine cents lower at A$2.56, well below the A$2.85 reached just after the deal's announcement.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
